courses.fullProfile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courses.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

courses.fullProfile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.

courses.fullProfile: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives.
courses.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

courses.fullProfile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courses.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.

courses.fullProfile: o What is the nature of consciousness? o What explains the identity of selves over time? How have different philosophical traditions thought about this issue? o Can the mind be explained in neurobiological terms? o Are large language models conscious? Can they ever be? o What can we learn from dream states about conscious experience? o What can perceptual illusions teach us about our awareness of the world? o What are the differences between human and animal consciousness? These are some of the questions explored in the philosophy of mind, an important field of philosophy since early modernity. The field has come to prominence and maturation in the past decades alongside advances in the scientific study of the human mind, research on animal minds, and innovations in computing. In this course, we will focus both on important work from the history of the field and on contributions from recent scholarship. We shall begin with exploration of the nature of selves and personal identity, looking at historical sources in the Western tradition, contemporary debate, as well as the theory of the self in Buddhist thought. Detailed discussion of approaches to the mind-body problem, a key issue in the philosophy of mind, will follow. Additional topics to be examined in the course include: the possibility of intelligent and conscious machines, animal minds, dream states, the significance of transformative experiences, and the impact of novel technologies on the ways we experience the world.
courses.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

courses.fullProfile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
courses.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

courses.fullProfile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
courses.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

courses.fullProfile: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courses.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

courses.fullProfile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
courses.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.

courses.fullProfile: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
courses.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

courses.fullProfile: This course builds upon the knowledge gained in the introductory course in Cognitive Science. It will deepen your knowledge of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Also, your knowledge of experimental approaches in the field of cognitive neuroscience will be enhanced; such that you become able to evaluate research findings and to design your own experiments. A selected number of higher order cognitive processes will be dealt with, including memory, emotion, social cognition, attention, consciousness, decision making and planning. In addition to established knowledge, current research questions will be discussed in depth.
courses.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.

courses.fullProfile: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.
courses.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.

courses.fullProfile: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16
courses.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

courses.fullProfile: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
courses.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

courses.fullProfile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
courses.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.

courses.fullProfile: The definition of what is a mental disorder is very complex, and there is no universal agreement about it. This course explores mental health and mental disorders across the lifespan, emphasizing a bio-psycho-social perspective that considers how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to promote mental health or contribute to the development of disorders. Students are introduced to historical and contemporary views of psychopathology, the prevalence and development of mental disorders, and the role of culture, gender, and environmental factors in shaping mental health and illness. The course familiarizes students with key concepts, terminology, theories, and research methods in psychopathology, while fostering critical thinking and analytical skills for evaluating mental health information. It addresses the assessment, diagnosis, classification, and treatment of mental disorders, including the most prevalent disorders from infancy through adulthood. Through interactive lectures, audiovisual materials, discussions, exercises, and written assignments, students gain a research-oriented understanding of maladaptive behavior and develop greater awareness of both their own mental health and the mental health of others within a comprehensive bio-psycho-social framework.
courses.description2: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.

courses.fullProfile: In th is course, Medical and Health Psychology , we will examine the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and socio-cultural factors that influence health and illness. Guided by the core principle of the field, the bio-psycho-social approach of the human being, we will explore key theories, research findings, and specific interventions within clinical health psychology, with a particular focus on the role of psychological expertise and mental health professionals in medical settings. Based on the World Health Organization’s (1948) definition of Health as a state of physical, mental and social well-being with a special emphasis in the balance between these aspects , Health Psychology is concerned with the elements that influence health and illness across the individual lifespan. It considers the implication of multiple aspects that can be combined in a complex way to promote and maintain health or to contribute for the settlement of dysfunction or illness. Therefore, This course will provide stude nts with a comprehensive understanding of these determinants and factors by addressing the following core areas: 1) Attitudes, behavior and lifestyle factors affecting health and disease; 2) Stress and the related psychosocial factors and processes associated with disease development and progression; Course outline HCBPSYC311 Medical & Health Psychology Page 2 of 11 3) Biopsychosocial factors involved in the illness experience; as well as, the long -term social and psychological implications of chronic illness; 4) Relevance of psychological interventions in medical…
courses.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.

courses.fullProfile: The main goal of this course is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and methods in the field of Clinical Psychology, which is concerned mainly with its scopes, functions and practices, reviewing the most important theoretical and practical perspectives in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies. Therefore, this course will address the following subject ar¬eas: Contemporary views in Clinical Psychology, including psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 1. Ethical issues in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 2. Mental Health intervention processes: Psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 3. Clinical psychological assessment: Psychodiagnostics; 4. Psychological assessment in infants, children, adolescents and adults; 5. Clinical psychological interventions and treatments: Different approaches in psychotherapy; 6. Some Clinical Psychology specialties in individual and group psychotherapeutic treatments for infants, children, adolescents and adults. Another objective of the course is to promote the development of critical thinking in the field of Clinical Psychology, especially in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies, to prepare the students to be cautious and analytical consumers of information on matters related to these topics.
courses.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.

courses.fullProfile: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
courses.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.

courses.fullProfile: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
courses.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

courses.fullProfile: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
courses.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.

courses.fullProfile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
courses.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

courses.fullProfile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
courses.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

courses.fullProfile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
courses.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
